newsitem.title: USA: Baxter wins ruling in CellPro dispute.
newsitem.headline: Baxter wins ruling in CellPro dispute.

text.p: A federal judge handed CellPro Inc a stunning defeat Thursday in a patent-infringement dispute with Baxter Healthcare Corp.

A ruling by Judge Roderick McKelvie of the U.S. District Court of Delaware limits CellPro's ability to make a bone-marrow transplant system and awards triple damages of $7.0 million to Baxter for CellPro's alleged willful infringement of one of its patents.

In the latest ruling on a case that began in 1994, McKelvie also ordered CellPro to pay Baxter, "60 percent of all incremental profits earned on sales of disposable products for the Ceprate SC" cancer treatment system.

McKelvie also denied CellPro's request that he not implement his orders while the company appeals his original finding that CellPro blood separation devices infringe Johns Hopkins' patents for purifying stem cells used in bone marrow transplants. Johns Hopkins licensed its patent rights to Becton Dickinson and Co, which in turn licensed them to Baxter.

McKelvie said: "CellPro argues that the terms of the permanent injunction will harm its ability to survive as a company...and to sell products that would serve public health interests...(but) CellPro's shut down' arguments are speculative at best.

"CellPro is a relatively small company when compared to the plaintiffs, but it has substantial resources. It has raised over $160 million in two public offerings and, as of December 31, 1996, it has $60 million available in cash and marketable securities."

In his ruling McKelvie said that while CellPro's strategy was, "to hold itself out as a warrior in a twentieth-century holy crusade...this image is a facade constructed by the venture capitalists who started this business. Behind the science, the medicine and the potential for treating cancer patients are investors who have demonstrated that their primary motivation is not humanitarianism...(but) greed."
A CellPro spokeswoman told Reuters the company has not yet read all four separate decisions by McKelvie, but continues to "feel very confident of our chances on appeal."

Still pending is a decision by Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala on whether CellPro's Ceprate systems qualify for a license under the Bayh-Dole Act as a product with a compelling public interest that was developed by federally-funded research.
